content: Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by a cycle of recurrent airway infections, inflammation, and subsequent tissue damage. Antibiotics play a central role in managing this condition. Continuous antibiotic therapy, which involves the prolonged use of prophylactic antibiotics, aims to suppress bacterial load in the airways. However, this approach carries the risk of promoting bacterial resistance, which can render the antibiotics less effective over time. Alternatively, intermittent antibiotic therapy involves administering antibiotics for predefined durations and intervals. This strategy may help reduce the selective pressure on bacteria, potentially lowering the risk of resistance development. The purpose of this systematic review was to assess the available evidence comparing continuous and intermittent antibiotic regimens in individuals with bronchiectasis. The review focused on key outcomes, including the frequency of exacerbations, the emergence of antibiotic resistance, and the occurrence of serious adverse events. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted on multiple databases, including the Cochrane Airways Review Group Specialised Register (CAGR), CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and AMED, on two separate occasions (August 1, 2017, and May 4, 2018). Additional searches were performed on clinical trial registries, such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization (WHO) trials portal, as well as conference proceedings and reference lists of existing systematic reviews. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults or children with bronchiectasis. These trials needed to compare continuous versus intermittent administration of long-term prophylactic antibiotics, with a minimum treatment duration of three months. Studies were considered eligible regardless of whether they were published as full-text articles, abstracts, or unpublished data. Two independent reviewers screened the search results and assessed the full-text reports for eligibility. Out of 268 unique records identified, 126 full-text reports representing 114 studies were examined. However, none of these studies met the inclusion criteria for the review. The authors concluded that no randomized controlled trials have been conducted to directly compare the effectiveness and risks of continuous versus intermittent antibiotic therapy in bronchiectasis. High-quality clinical trials are urgently needed to determine which approach is more effective in reducing exacerbation frequency and duration, minimizing antibiotic resistance, and preventing serious adverse events.
